summary: Defines new TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 cipher suites that combine ephemeral elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman with a pre-shared key for key exchange, using AES-GCM and AES-CCM authenticated encryption. They suit devices that share a secret in advance and still want fresh session keys.

eli5.summary: Two friends already know a secret handshake, and they also make up a new secret code for each chat. These are new recipes for doing both.

questions: tls psk with aes-gcm and aes-ccm
which tls cipher suites use psk with aes-gcm
can ecdhe_psk suites be used with tls 1.3
subtitle: Four TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 cipher suites that pair a pre-shared key with ephemeral elliptic-curve key exchange and AEAD encryption.

tldr.problem: Existing PSK cipher suites for TLS either lack elliptic curves or lack ECDHE with AES-GCM and AES-CCM, so no suite offered PSK authentication, forward secrecy and AEAD together.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8442 defines four cipher suites that use the ECDHE_PSK key exchange from RFC 5489 with AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, AES-128-CCM and AES-128-CCM-8.
tldr.outcome: The suites give confidentiality, mutual authentication and forward secrecy for TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 only. TLS 1.3 gets equivalent functionality through its own suites.

today: RFC 8442 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2018. The metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why These Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The document defines cipher suites that provide pre-shared key (PSK) authentication, perfect forward secrecy (PFS) and authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD). They are defined for TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) and DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347).

The RFC says PSK authentication is widely used. It names 3GPP networks, where pre-shared keys authenticate both subscriber and network, and the Internet of Things, where PSK is often preferred for performance and energy efficiency. In both cases the endpoints are owned or controlled by a party that provisions keys with a high level of entropy.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets already share a secret with the server. They still want a fresh secret every time they talk, in case someone steals the old one later.

sections.title: The Gap in Earlier Specifications
sections.content:
Each earlier document covered only part of the combination. RFC 4279 defines PSK cipher suites but not elliptic curves. RFC 8422 adds elliptic curves but not PSK. RFC 5487 combines AES-GCM with PSK but has no ECDHE. RFC 5489 combines PSK with ECDHE but has no AES-GCM or AES-CCM.

ECDHE gives PFS with excellent performance and small key sizes, and it is mandatory to implement in HTTP/2 and CoAP. AEAD algorithms are strongly recommended for TLS and DTLS, and TLS 1.3 forbids non-AEAD algorithms.
sections.eli5: Each older recipe had some of the ingredients, but none had all three: the shared secret, the fresh secret and the strong lock.

sections.title: How the Suites Are Built
sections.content:
The suites use four AEAD algorithms: AEAD_AES_128_GCM, AEAD_AES_256_GCM, AEAD_AES_128_CCM and AEAD_AES_128_CCM_8.

Message and premaster secret construction follow RFC 5489. The ServerKeyExchange and ClientKeyExchange messages are used, and the premaster secret is computed as for the ECDHE_PSK key exchange. The elliptic curve parameters are negotiated with the extensions from RFC 8422.
sections.eli5: The suites reuse the existing handshake recipe and just swap in modern locks to protect the messages.

sections.title: The Four Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Four suites are defined, with code points in the 0xD0 range: TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_SHA256.

All four are marked DTLS-OK. The IANA table marks all except the CCM_8 suite as Recommended.
sections.eli5: There are four ready-made recipes with different lock sizes. The one with the small lock is not recommended.

sections.title: TLS 1.2 Only
sections.content:
The assigned code points can only be used for TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2. The suites MUST NOT be negotiated for any other version of (D)TLS, and servers MUST NOT select one of them when choosing another version.

A client MUST treat such a selection as an error and generate a fatal illegal_parameter alert. For TLS 1.3, the suites TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 and TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256 support equivalent functionality.
sections.eli5: These recipes only work for one version of the handshake. If a server picks one for the wrong version, the client stops the conversation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of TLS 1.2, DTLS 1.2, PSK ciphersuites, ECDHE_PSK, AES-GCM and AES-CCM all apply. All the suites provide confidentiality, mutual authentication and forward secrecy. The AES-128 suites provide 128-bit security and the AES-256 suites provide at least 192-bit security. However, AES_128_CCM_8 only provides 64-bit security against message forgery.

The pre-shared keys MUST have a security level equal to or higher than the suite used: at least 128-bit for AES-128 suites and at least 192-bit for AES-256 suites. GCM and CCM MUST only be used with a system guaranteeing nonce uniqueness, because reusing a nonce with the same key undermines their security.
sections.eli5: A lock is only as good as the key. The shared secret must be at least as strong as the lock, and you must never reuse a one-time number.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The four values were assigned in the TLS Cipher Suites registry defined by RFC 8446 and RFC 8447. They are {0xD0,0x01}, {0xD0,0x02}, {0xD0,0x03} and {0xD0,0x05}.
sections.eli5: Each recipe gets its own number in the official list so both sides can name the one they want.
